newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bankers doubt their vaults hold Mobutu money.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bankers doubt their vaults hold Mobutu money.

text.p: Swiss banks are unlikely to hold much money from embattled Zairean strongman Mobutu Sese Seko because of the severe damage their business and image would suffer if the dealings became public, bankers said on Friday.
"Any bank that has this kind of money in this day and age is either foolish or very daring," Swiss Bankers Association spokeswoman Silvia Matile told Reuters.

The Swiss government ordered a freeze on a luxury villa owned by Mobutu but said Zaire prosecutors had not provided enough details to allow the seizure of any other Mobutu assets, estimated by the Swiss media to have once totalled $4 billion.
Federal banking watchdogs have also ordered banks to report any Mobutu wealth they might hold after an initial informal survey last month turned up no leads.

Private bankers, whose business is based on wooing wealthy customers to hand over their fortunes for managing, agreed that the risk of being branded a partner to dictators made business with Mobutu too dangerous.
"It doesn't make business sense," one banker active in asset management said on condition he not be named.
"Once confronted with this kind of deal in public, the damage to a bank's name, it business and goodwill would be enormous," the banker added.
Swiss banks are routinely accused of holding the treasures of toppled dictators.

But a top executive at one of Switzerland's biggest banks said they had learned lessons from scandals surrounding accounts found in the late 1980s from ousted leaders Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines and Haiti's Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier.
"You can never make as much money from this kind of client as you lose on legal fees, public relations work and top management time in the aftermath," the executive told Reuters.

Rules on monitoring the integrity of customers have become strict since the late 1980s, partly in response to the Marcos case and partly due to world-wide moves by financial regulators to block the laundering of criminal profits.
The Marcos case has been the biggest in recent years, involving accounts now totalling some $500 million at two of Switzerland's biggest banks -- Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) and Credit Suisse Group.
Berne ordered the accounts frozen shortly after Marcos was toppled in 1986. The new Philippines administration claimed Marcos' fortunes were stolen from the country.
But the accounts are still tied up in complex legal wrangling between the Philippines government, the Marcos family and victims of Marcos persecution.
Haiti sought the return of Duvalier's wealth after he was ousted in 1986.
Officials found a few million Swiss francs in Zurich and Geneva accounts, but their repatriation has since bogged down as Berne waits for a Haitian guarantee of fair legal proceedings.
Last month, justice officials said they would return 3.2 million Swiss francs to Mali that the west African state's authorities say former dictator Moussa Traore stole.
This will be the first time that Switzerland has handed over money from a toppled head of state based on claims by a successor government that the cash was obtained illegally.
Mali's new government asked Switzerland to freeze and return funds after the military ousted Traore in 1991 and paved the way for multi-party democracy.
Other hunts for rulers' fortunes have been less rewarding.
No traces of fortunes reputedly stashed in Switzerland by Romanian strongman Nicolae Ceaucescu were ever found.
Bulgaria's communist dictator Todor Zhivkov, ousted by his party in 1989, was rumoured to have money in Switzerland but Bulgaria never sought legal help to find it.
